chapters.title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: “Ah.”
I blinked. It was hot and humid. When I exhaled, my breath fogged my vision. I felt around my head and touched something hard.
The VR helmet.
I pulled it off, revealing the dusty interior of the capsule.
I sat in the old capsule chair with its worn-flat cushions and waited for my pounding heart to calm down.
Reality? Is this really reality?
Logout after exactly thirty days. Fear surged through me.
Was this really the real world? When I pressed that button and the capsule opened, would I find that too much had changed?
Heart trembling, I opened my mouth.
“Open Status Window.”
Silence.
Neither the familiar notification nor the System Window answered.
Only then did it finally sink in.
I had successfully logged out.
“Huuup.”
I drew a deep breath and pressed the button. The capsule door opened with a click, and stale air greeted me.
A dark, cramped room. A small TV on the desk. A single bed. And one person asleep on it, reeking of alcohol.
“Khrrr. Khrrooo.”
Who would’ve thought those bizarre snores could sound so welcome?
I’m back. Back in reality.
Everything was exactly as I remembered it. The last thirty days felt like a dream.
After staring blankly around the room for a while, I walked over to Jinho hyung. Then I slammed the edge of my hand into his uvula.
Whack!
“Khrrr... gack!”
If it hadn’t been for this guy’s snoring, I never would have crawled into that capsule. I grabbed Jinho tight as he thrashed around.
“Take one more. No, two.”
Whack! Whack!
“Gack! Grrrgh!”
“You’re both old enough to know better. Especially you, when you’re supposed to be the goshiwon manager.”
“...Sorry.”
“Let’s not have any more embarrassing scenes, all right?”
Bang.
The door closed. Jinho turned around with a sigh.
“Are you insane?”
Before he could say anything worse, I beat him to the punch.
“For the record, it was self-defense.”
“What the fuck are you talking about? Have you lost your mind?”
“I’m perfectly sane.”
“Then why the hell did you hit someone in the throat while he was sleeping—!”
Thump, thump, thump.
The man next door pounded on the wall. Judging by the rhythm and force, the message was clear: I want to kill you.
Jinho lowered his voice.
“Why the hell did you pull that shit? In the middle of the night, too.”
“The middle of the night?”
“Yeah, you lunatic. It’s only three in the morning.”
Jinho held out his phone, looking utterly dumbfounded.
July 25. 3:02 a.m.
I checked the date and time, and my mouth fell open.
Only three hours have passed?
I’d spent a whole month in Murim. Exactly thirty days. Yet only three hours had passed in reality.
“...Hyung.”
“Don’t talk to me. My throat hurts.”
“What’s the usual time ratio for a game capsule?”
“You’re like Hong Gil-dong, you bastard—popping up in the east one moment and the west the next. Even your conversation topics are all over the place.”
“What’s the ratio?”
“Huh?”
When I asked with a stiff face, Jinho hyung looked briefly flustered, then answered.
“The latest capsule that came out last month can do five to one, I think.”
“What exactly does five to one mean?”
“What do you think? Five hours pass in the game for every hour in reality.”
This was driving me crazy.
“What about anything beyond that?”
“There isn’t anything. Five to one is the limit of current technology... But why are you asking?”
Because something impossible had happened.
How am I supposed to make sense of this?
Even at a second glance, the capsule was ancient. That piece of junk, made more than twenty years ago, had left modern technology in the dust.
Thirty days in only three hours. What kind of time ratio was that? My head was too scrambled even to calculate it.
“That’s insane.”
“What is?”
There was no way I could understand this on my own. Maybe Jinho could come up with some kind of answer.
After a moment’s hesitation, I spoke.
“A month ago—no, three hours ago—I went into that capsule...”
I’d been through so much that there was a lot to tell. Even after hearing the whole story, Jinho remained silent for a long time.
Then he said one thing.
“That’s insane.”
“Exactly. How does any of this make sense? Could that be some illegally modified capsule or something?”
“No. Not the capsule. You.”
“Huh?”
Jinho hyung spoke with a serious face.
“Just own it and apologize. Say, ‘I’m sorry. Your snoring was so loud I hit you.’ Be cool about it, you bastard.”
“What, you couldn’t log out and spent a month risking your life in a game? Go write a novel.”
Right. I knew that was going too well.
I sighed.
“I’m telling you, it’s true.”
“Come on, Taekyung. Let’s think about this rationally.”
Jinho put on a solemn tone.

“Some guy smacks a sleeping person in the uvula to wake him up, then says he was trapped in a game for a month. But he checks the clock, and only three hours have passed? And the capsule is an antique that belongs in a museum?”
“I know it sounds insane. I get it. But...”
“Then try to get me, too. My head hurts from the hangover, my uvula hurts, and looking at you hurts.”
“No, just listen to me!”
Thump, thump, thump, thump.
Before the man next door could smash through the wall, I lowered my voice.
“Then try it yourself.”
“What?”
“If you try it, you’ll believe me.”
Nothing was faster than experiencing it firsthand. If I pulled him out after about ten minutes, he’d have no choice but to believe me.
Jinho stared hard at me before answering.
“Fine. Let’s try it, then.”
He climbed into the capsule and even put on the VR helmet. As he grumbled about the sour smell inside it, I said,
“I’ll pull you out soon. Stay holed up at Honghwaru.”
“Honghwaru, my ass. Just close the capsule door.”
I was curious to see his face when he came back out. I closed the capsule door, took out my phone, and opened the stopwatch.
The instant I pressed start, the numbers began racing upward.
One second, two seconds... ten seconds.
Ten seconds in reality had to mean minutes, maybe even hours, in the game.
By now, he must be scrambling to figure out what’s going on at Honghwaru...
Clunk.
“Huh?”
The door opened.
What? Why is he already out? No, how did he get out?
Jinho sighed at my bewildered expression.
“What are you doing?”
“Uh... Huh?”
“The power isn’t even on. What game were you playing?”
What was that supposed to mean?
“The power isn’t on?”
“Move.”
While I was still stammering, Jinho climbed out of the capsule, bent down, and picked something up from underneath it.
“What does this look like to you?”
A cord.
An unplugged power cord.
I scrubbed furiously at my eyes, but nothing changed.
Was I seeing things?
“Why is this...”
“Taekyung. Jin Taekyung. You poor, pathetic soul.”
Jinho gazed at me with sorrowful eyes.
“Go to a mental hospital as soon as the sun comes up. I’m going back to my room.”
He tossed the power cord aside and walked away. I stared blankly after him.
The power cord hadn’t even been plugged in.
Then what was the game I played?
I felt as though I’d been bewitched by a ghost. Goose bumps rose all over my body.
I lay on the bed and thought.
Am I crazy?
I’d played a game for thirty days in a capsule that hadn’t even been plugged in.
I could understand Jinho’s reaction. But everything that had happened there...
It was all real.
Jin Wikyung, Wolhwa, Hyuk Mujin, and the Head Elder. I remembered every NPC’s face, their way of speaking, their mannerisms. It hadn’t been a delusion I’d cooked up on my own.
Then what was the problem?
There was only one answer.
The problem was the game capsule itself. It had been made twenty-seven years ago—a piece of junk that should have been retired long ago and put in a museum.
Even its date of manufacture was suspicious.
January 1, 2020.
The day the Demon King Asmodeus fell at humanity’s hands.
Who the hell was making game capsules back then?
Hundreds of millions had died during the five-year Great War, and monsters had roamed through city centers.
In my opinion, the bastards who heard the breaking news that the Demon King had fallen and fired up a factory going, All right, let’s make game capsules now! belonged in court.
Back then, I thought it was a misprint.
I froze.
A misprint?
The product manual!
How could I have forgotten something that important? What an idiot.
I shot to my feet and began turning the room upside down. At last, I found the familiar little booklet under the bed.
Product User Manual Product Name: Virtual Reality Access Device Model Name: Ark - 2020 Manufacturer: H Soft Date of Manufacture: January 1, 2020
Then the next page.
Precautions The player cannot log out at will. - If the player dies during play, resurrection is impossible.
A month ago—no, three hours ago—I had thrown the booklet aside at this point.
This time was different.
With trembling hands, I turned to the last page.

Key Features A custom capsule made for one person only! Once a user is registered, the capsule is permanently bound to that user until death. - Time-ratio adjustment for comfortable play! Upon login, time in reality passes very slowly. The reverse is also true. - Character Synchronization System! By synchronizing with their character, the user experiences a greater sense of unity.
“What the hell is this?”
I could read the words, but my brain refused to process them. I started again from the beginning.
First, permanent binding.
It meant exactly what it said. The capsule was mine until I died. Once I got some answers, I was going to smash the goddamn thing to pieces.
Next, the time ratio.
That was the part I’d been most curious about. But instead of an exact figure, all it gave me was the vague phrase passes very slowly.
It said the reverse was also true, so time in the game must be passing very slowly now.
Then is the war still going on?

Jin Wikyung came to mind. The Head Elder’s betrayal was already a given, and he would try to stab Wikyung in the back at the critical moment. Had Hyuk Mujin and the reconnaissance squad gotten that news to him?
Right. That’s still a long way off. The time ratio reversed.
More importantly, I had immediate problems of my own. I examined the final key feature, but unlike the others, this one made no sense no matter how many times I read it.
Synchronize with a character?
Just to be sure, I even looked it up in a Korean dictionary. It meant exactly what I thought it meant, which only made it sound even crazier.
How the hell do you synchronize with a game character?
I couldn’t make any sense of it. In the end, all I’d done was add another question to the pile.
One thing was certain.
I wasn’t crazy.
I flopped onto the bed and read the front of the booklet again.
“Manufacturer: H Soft.”
In the end, every road led to the same place. If I investigated these bastards, something was bound to turn up.
I searched the internet for H Soft, but aside from a porn studio with the same name, I didn’t find a thing.
First, I needed to lock the door and think.

chapters.title: Chapter 40
paragraphs: I was flying through the sky. With my enormous wings spread wide, I cut through the wind.
Far below lay a high, steep gorge shaped like a bottle gourd. Hundreds of people stood within it.
A man standing at the center shouted at the top of his lungs.
“Don’t fight for the Jin Family of Taiyuan!”
Then the ground shook. Trees trembled, and mountain birds took flight.
I glanced behind me. A massive cloud of dust was sweeping through the gorge toward us.
“Fight for yourselves! Fight for your families and the ones you love, before the enemy tramples them!”
He drew his sword and roared.
“Stand and face them like martial artists! I will do the same!”
Hundreds of weapons were drawn in unison. The man strode forward and took the lead. The cloud of dust crossing the gorge scattered, revealing countless people.
“Waaaaah!”
“Wipe out those Jin Family bastards!”
The man suddenly looked up. When he spotted me, he grinned.
“I’ve got a good feeling about this.”
The moment I saw his face, the strength drained from my wings. I plummeted into the depths of my consciousness.
“Pwah! Pwah-pwah!”
I desperately flapped my wings—or rather, my arms—before realizing what had happened.
It was a dream.
Thank god. I thought I was a goner. Only after catching my breath did the situation in the room come into focus.
“This is a breaking news report. A new Gate has appeared at Exit 3 of Hapjeong Station. Magical power measurements have confirmed it as a Grade C Gate, and...”
A small TV sat on the desk, showing an announcer. And then there was—
“What the hell was that?”
Jinho hyung stood there with a pot lid in one hand and chopsticks in the other, staring at me like I was out of my mind.
“Some kind of performance art?”
“Shut up. I was dreaming.”
“About swimming?”
“About falling.”
“Good for you. You’ll grow taller.”
He delivered the line without a shred of interest and slurped up his noodles, looking completely at home. For a moment, I wondered if this was even my room.
“This is my room, right?”
“Probably.”
“Then why are you here?”
“Is this anything new?”
That actually sounded plausible. I almost bought it.
“Turn off the TV or something. People are trying to sleep.”
“Some inconsiderate bastard even hits people in the uvula while they’re sleeping.”
Anyway, that bastard had one hell of a mouth on him.
“If you’ve got nothing to say, eat some ramen. I cooked five packs because I thought you might wake up.”
Talk about foresight. I took the chopsticks from him, overcome with emotion.
This wasn’t just ordinary ramen. It was my first ramen in a month.
The smell that pulled at my appetite. Noodles cooked just right. Broth boiled spicy with separately sliced Cheongyang peppers.
This is insane. Absolutely insane.
Slurp.
By the time I came to my senses, it was all over. Jinho stared blankly as I licked the pot clean.
“I thought you were filming a commercial. Have you never eaten ramen in your life?”
“It’s my first ramen since I came back.”
“Are you still on that?”
“Try eating nothing but Chinese food for a month, then have some ramen. Michelin’s got nothing on this.”
“Stop. It’s not funny anymore.”
He looked thoroughly fed up. This time, though, I had something to back up my story.
“Look this over, then we’ll talk.”
“What’s this?”
“What do you think? A product user manual.”
“...Don’t tell me.”
“Yeah. It was inside that capsule. Read it.”
“Someone left this inside when they threw out a piece of junk more than twenty years old?”
Jinho tilted his head, then started reading. A few seconds later, he looked up.
“This is a misprint. The date of manufacture says January 1, 2020.”
I’d thought the same thing at first.
At first.
“That might not be a printing error.”
“Huh?”
“No, forget it. That’s still just a guess. What about the rest? Have you heard of the model or the manufacturer listed there?”
Jinho was crazy about electronics, especially capsules.
He was a well-known user on all the relevant sites and had even run an IT blog.
But his immediate answer sent my expectations crashing down.
“No.”
Well, that was only natural. Even an internet search hadn’t turned anything up. Still, I couldn’t help feeling a little disappointed.
“You really don’t know? You know this field inside out.”
“Yeah. But I don’t know this.”
Jinho scratched his head.
“An illegally modified capsule? Or maybe a custom job? Honestly, I’ve never seen a design like that.”
The more he talked, the bleaker it sounded.
“Fine, forget the design. But I know every model from the very first to the latest—everything that’s ever been released in Korea.”
“And?”
“The model name written here. The manufacturer. I’ve never seen either of them in my life.”
“Couldn’t it be an overseas manufacturer?”
“Oh, you hopeless idiot. You dumbass. You moron.”
Looking thoroughly exasperated, Jinho thrust the manual at me.
“Read the first line.”
“Product User Manual?”
“Exactly. It’s in Korean. Korean!”
“Oh.”

“Whether H Soft is a domestic company or a foreign one, if they went to the trouble of producing a Korean manual, there’s no way I wouldn’t know them. It’s not like there are hundreds or thousands of capsule manufacturers out there.”
I felt like a complete idiot. Not that I knew anything about capsules in the first place.
Then Jinho spoke up.
“Wait a second.”
He pulled out his smartphone and started tapping the screen. He seemed to be searching, but the result was obvious.
“Fuck. All I’m getting is porn sites.”
Yeah, that one was pretty good.
“It’s not even a ghost company. Why is there nothing about it?”
“Read the rest too.”
By the time he reached the last page, he’d really feel like he’d been haunted. Jinho turned the pages with a serious expression.
Once.
Then again.
“Isn’t it incredible?”
“Yeah. Incredible.”
His voice was hollow.
“You told me to look at blank pages. That’s incredible.”
“Huh?”
“No wonder I thought this manual was so half-assed. No explanation of the capsule’s components, no operating instructions, and even the model name, manufacturer, and date of manufacture are a mess.”
“Blank pages? What are you talking about?”
“Well, well. Look at this humanities-major bastard playing innocent.”
I snatched the manual from him and hurriedly read it.
The contents I’d seen before falling asleep were still there. Precautions on the second page. Key features on the last.
“You can’t see this?”
“Knock it off. This is starting to scare me.”
That expression. That tone.
He meant it.
The writing I could see was invisible to Jinho.
Or maybe...
Only I can see it.
I remained frozen for a long time.
Pshhh—
I climbed out of the capsule on shaky legs.
Its glossy exterior made it look like a giant egg. This was the latest model, released only last month.
“Oh, you’re out already. Did you try the game I recommended?”
Still half out of my mind, I answered the capsule café owner sitting behind the counter.
“Yes.”
The virtual-reality game he’d recommended was a megahit with ten million concurrent users. He’d said it had incredible graphics, outstanding freedom, and more than seventy percent of the market.
“The graphics are insane, right?”
I logged into the game, saw the graphics, and thought:
Am I the one who’s insane?
This is the most popular virtual-reality game out there?
The graphics were good. I could give it that.
But that was as far as it went.
The NPCs’ faces and movements. Their dialogue patterns. All five senses as I experienced them through my character. All of it felt unnatural.
It was a game. It never felt like reality.
“Do you have any wuxia games?”
“Ah, so that’s what you’re into? There are quite a few. What’s the title you’re looking for?”
“Murim.”
“Murim Online?”
“No. It’s an open-world game. Single-player.”
“Is there a wuxia game like that?”
Figures.
There was nothing more to hear. I staggered out the door, and the owner called after me.
“Come again!”
I wouldn’t.
Not ever again.
Hope Goshiwon.
I sat beneath the old, rusted sign and pulled out my smartphone. The other end picked up almost before it could ring.
Click.
“Yeah. What?”
My one and only nemesis—no, my younger sister, Hayeon.
The moment I heard that uniquely bratty voice of hers, my throat closed up.
“Hello?”
“...Yeah.”
“Why’d you call?”
“Just because. I wanted to hear your voice.”
A deathly silence followed.
“I’m hanging up.”
“No, wait. Wait!”
“You have three seconds. What do you want?”
That damn girl...
Right. This was Jin Hayeon.
Thanks to her, my tear ducts, which had gotten a little moist, dried out like the sand around the pyramids.
“What’s Mom doing?”
“She went out on an errand. Call her if you’re curious.”
I deliberately hadn’t called her. Hearing this brat’s voice was already enough to choke me up. If I heard Mom’s, I might start bawling like a little kid.
I quickly changed the subject.
“What about you?”
“What do you think a high-school senior with a hundred and twenty days left until the college entrance exam is doing? Studying.”
Her tone was sharper than usual. Exam stress must have been getting to her.
“How’s studying going?”
“I bombed the July mock exam. I didn’t manage my condition right and missed even the easy questions. God, the more I think about it, the more annoyed I get.”
“It’s fine. Just do well on the real thing. How many did you miss?”
“Two.”
“That’s still Grade 1. What about the other subjects?”
“Two across all subjects.”
“Huh?”
“One in Korean history and one in math.”
“...Two total? Across every subject? Are you serious?”
“Obviously that’s what I meant.”
Smart little brat...
I knew she was good at studying, but I hadn’t realized she was this good. Thinking back on my own school grades, it really seemed like there was such a thing as dumping all the genes into one kid.
“You’re pretty good at this studying thing, huh?”
“From your perspective, aren’t I amazing?”
“W-what kind of nonsense is that? I was pretty good at studying too, you know. You just don’t remember because you were in elementary school...”
“Last week during a deep clean, I found your report card. There were so many Grade 7s I thought it was a slot machine that had hit the jackpot.”
“You need some allowance, right? How much does makeup cost these days?”
“That’s pathetic. Seriously.”

I found myself getting oddly sentimental.
I really did come back.
Had I been dreaming? Or had I lost myself in some delusion?
Only a day had passed in reality, yet utterly incomprehensible, inexplicable things had happened.
But I decided not to try to understand them anymore.
I’m back in reality now.
And this was where I had to live.
My family was here. I was here. That was enough.
I’d simply had a strange dream for a little while. The kind of dream that would naturally fade with time.
“Yeah.”
Listening to my little sister chatter, I got to my feet.
It was time to leave the old, rusted sign behind and return to my room.
Bzzzt. Bzzzt.

Six in the morning.
The signal that his day had begun.
“Oh, I’m dying.”
It had been five years since he left home. By now, the moldy smell that crept into his nose every morning had become thoroughly familiar.
Eyes half closed, Seong Jinho shoved his cigarettes and lighter into his pocket and left the room.
Nothing wakes you up like a cigarette.
He shuffled up to the rooftop in his slippers. Just as he put a cigarette between his lips—
Thud.
“Huh?”
What was that?
He leaned over the railing and spotted a hunk of metal in the recycling area directly below.
He also saw the well-built young man standing there, staring at it.
“Hey! Jin Taekyung!”
At Seong Jinho’s shout, Jin Taekyung looked up.
“What?”
“You throwing that away?”
The hunk of metal was the junk capsule Taekyung had picked up the day before. After pulling that ridiculous prank with it, he seemed to be taking it right back out to the trash.
He was awfully serious for a prank, though... Ah, whatever. It was all nonsense.
Seong Jinho let out a short laugh.
“Why throw it away? Aren’t you going back to Murim?”
“You believed that?”
Jin Taekyung smiled back. But to Seong Jinho, who had watched him for a long time, the smile looked somehow awkward.
What’s with him?
Something felt off.
Jin Taekyung waved to the uneasy Seong Jinho and started down the hill.
“Where are you going, you punk? Aren’t we having breakfast together later?”
“I have to work!”
Jin Taekyung left without looking back. Seong Jinho took a drag from his half-smoked cigarette.
“That bastard really works hard...”
Soon, Jin Taekyung disappeared from sight.
Seong Jinho stubbed out his cigarette in a flowerpot and was about to leave when the junk capsule caught his eye.
He said the manufacturer was H Soft, right?
It was probably just some half-assed prank, but there was no harm in looking into it.

sentences.text: I was flying through the sky.
With my enormous wings spread wide, I cut through the wind.
Far below lay a high, steep gorge shaped like a bottle gourd.
Hundreds of people stood within it.
A man standing at the center shouted at the top of his lungs.

Trees trembled, and mountain birds took flight.
I glanced behind me.
A massive cloud of dust was sweeping through the gorge toward us.
“Fight for yourselves!
Fight for your families and the ones you love, before the enemy tramples them!”
He drew his sword and roared.
“Stand and face them like martial artists!
I will do the same!”
Hundreds of weapons were drawn in unison.
The man strode forward and took the lead.
The cloud of dust crossing the gorge scattered, revealing countless people.
“Waaaaah!”
“Wipe out those Jin Family bastards!”
The man suddenly looked up.
When he spotted me, he grinned.
“I’ve got a good feeling about this.”
The moment I saw his face, the strength drained from my wings.
I plummeted into the depths of my consciousness.
“Pwah!
Pwah-pwah!”
I desperately flapped my wings—or rather, my arms—before realizing what had happened.
It was a dream.
Thank god.
I thought I was a goner.
Only after catching my breath did the situation in the room come into focus.
“This is a breaking news report.
A new Gate has appeared at Exit 3 of Hapjeong Station.
Magical power measurements have confirmed it as a Grade C Gate, and...”
A small TV sat on the desk, showing an announcer.
And then there was—
“What the hell was that?”
Jinho hyung stood there with a pot lid in one hand and chopsticks in the other, staring at me like I was out of my mind.
“Some kind of performance art?”
“Shut up.
I was dreaming.”
“About swimming?”
“About falling.”
“Good for you.
You’ll grow taller.”
He delivered the line without a shred of interest and slurped up his noodles, looking completely at home.
For a moment, I wondered if this was even my room.
“This is my room, right?”
“Probably.”
“Then why are you here?”
“Is this anything new?”
That actually sounded plausible.
I almost bought it.
“Turn off the TV or something.
People are trying to sleep.”
“Some inconsiderate bastard even hits people in the uvula while they’re sleeping.”
Anyway, that bastard had one hell of a mouth on him.
“If you’ve got nothing to say, eat some ramen.

Talk about foresight.
I took the chopsticks from him, overcome with emotion.
This wasn’t just ordinary ramen.
It was my first ramen in a month.
The smell that pulled at my appetite.
Noodles cooked just right.
Broth boiled spicy with separately sliced Cheongyang peppers.
This is insane.
Absolutely insane.
Slurp.
By the time I came to my senses, it was all over.
Jinho stared blankly as I licked the pot clean.
“I thought you were filming a commercial.
Have you never eaten ramen in your life?”
“It’s my first ramen since I came back.”
“Are you still on that?”
“Try eating nothing but Chinese food for a month, then have some ramen.
Michelin’s got nothing on this.”
“Stop.
It’s not funny anymore.”
He looked thoroughly fed up.
This time, though, I had something to back up my story.
“Look this over, then we’ll talk.”
“What’s this?”
“What do you think?
A product user manual.”
“...Don’t tell me.”
“Yeah.
It was inside that capsule.
Read it.”
“Someone left this inside when they threw out a piece of junk more than twenty years old?”
Jinho tilted his head, then started reading.
A few seconds later, he looked up.
“This is a misprint.
The date of manufacture says January 1, 2020.”
I’d thought the same thing at first.
At first.
“That might not be a printing error.”
“Huh?”
“No, forget it.
That’s still just a guess.
What about the rest?
Have you heard of the model or the manufacturer listed there?”
Jinho was crazy about electronics, especially capsules.
He was a well-known user on all the relevant sites and had even run an IT blog.
But his immediate answer sent my expectations crashing down.
“No.”
Well, that was only natural.
Even an internet search hadn’t turned anything up.
Still, I couldn’t help feeling a little disappointed.
“You really don’t know?
You know this field inside out.”
“Yeah.
But I don’t know this.”
Jinho scratched his head.
“An illegally modified capsule?
Or maybe a custom job?
Honestly, I’ve never seen a design like that.”
The more he talked, the bleaker it sounded.
“Fine, forget the design.
But I know every model from the very first to the latest—everything that’s ever been released in Korea.”
“And?”
“The model name written here.
The manufacturer.
I’ve never seen either of them in my life.”
“Couldn’t it be an overseas manufacturer?”
“Oh, you hopeless idiot.
You dumbass.
You moron.”
Looking thoroughly exasperated, Jinho thrust the manual at me.
“Read the first line.”
“Product User Manual?”
“Exactly.
It’s in Korean.
Korean!”
“Oh.”
“Whether H Soft is a domestic company or a foreign one, if they went to the trouble of producing a Korean manual, there’s no way I wouldn’t know them.
It’s not like there are hundreds or thousands of capsule manufacturers out there.”
I felt like a complete idiot.
Not that I knew anything about capsules in the first place.
Then Jinho spoke up.
“Wait a second.”
He pulled out his smartphone and started tapping the screen.
He seemed to be searching, but the result was obvious.
“Fuck.
All I’m getting is porn sites.”
Yeah, that one was pretty good.
“It’s not even a ghost company.
Why is there nothing about it?”
“Read the rest too.”
By the time he reached the last page, he’d really feel like he’d been haunted.
Jinho turned the pages with a serious expression.
Once.
Then again.
“Isn’t it incredible?”
“Yeah.
Incredible.”
His voice was hollow.
“You told me to look at blank pages.
That’s incredible.”
“Huh?”
“No wonder I thought this manual was so half-assed.
No explanation of the capsule’s components, no operating instructions, and even the model name, manufacturer, and date of manufacture are a mess.”
“Blank pages?
What are you talking about?”
“Well, well.
Look at this humanities-major bastard playing innocent.”
I snatched the manual from him and hurriedly read it.
The contents I’d seen before falling asleep were still there.
Precautions on the second page.
Key features on the last.
“You can’t see this?”
“Knock it off.
This is starting to scare me.”
That expression.
That tone.
He meant it.
The writing I could see was invisible to Jinho.
Or maybe...
Only I can see it.
I remained frozen for a long time.
Pshhh—
I climbed out of the capsule on shaky legs.
Its glossy exterior made it look like a giant egg.
This was the latest model, released only last month.
“Oh, you’re out already.
Did you try the game I recommended?”
Still half out of my mind, I answered the capsule café owner sitting behind the counter.
“Yes.”
The virtual-reality game he’d recommended was a megahit with ten million concurrent users.
He’d said it had incredible graphics, outstanding freedom, and more than seventy percent of the market.
“The graphics are insane, right?”
I logged into the game, saw the graphics, and thought:
Am I the one who’s insane?
This is the most popular virtual-reality game out there?
The graphics were good.
I could give it that.
But that was as far as it went.
The NPCs’ faces and movements.
Their dialogue patterns.
All five senses as I experienced them through my character.
All of it felt unnatural.
It was a game.
It never felt like reality.
“Do you have any wuxia games?”
“Ah, so that’s what you’re into?
There are quite a few.
What’s the title you’re looking for?”
“Murim.”
“Murim Online?”
“No.
It’s an open-world game.
Single-player.”
“Is there a wuxia game like that?”
Figures.
There was nothing more to hear.
I staggered out the door, and the owner called after me.
“Come again!”
I wouldn’t.
Not ever again.
Hope Goshiwon.
I sat beneath the old, rusted sign and pulled out my smartphone.
The other end picked up almost before it could ring.
Click.
“Yeah.
What?”
My one and only nemesis—no, my younger sister, Hayeon.

chapters.title: Chapter 41
paragraphs: The Hunter Manpower Office.
They called it an office, but it occupied an entire six-story building on prime real estate right by the station. Hundreds of Hunters passed through its doors every day.
It’s been a while.
Even at dawn, the lobby was packed.
After waiting through the long line, I reached the counter. The woman behind it asked in a businesslike tone,
“Is this your first time at the manpower office?”
“No. I’m already registered.”
“Your name?”
“Jin Taekyung.”

Back when I was a rookie, I’d graduated from the Hunter Training Center with excellent scores. But hardly anyone needed an F-rank Hunter like me, and the contracts a few small and midsize Guilds offered as if they were doing me a favor were highway robbery.
So I’d come here instead. To a different branch, though.
“There’s a record at the Ilsan branch. I’ve put you on the list, so please wait in the hall on the first floor.”
“Yes.”
This six-story building was a pyramid unto itself. The first floor took E- and F-ranks. You needed to be at least D-rank to set foot on the second.
Some people got angry and asked if that wasn’t blatant discrimination.
It was.
Not like this was the first or second time.
I’d lasted seven years in this business and seen every ugly side of it. I’d long since passed the point where I could afford to be picky.
I had just started walking when—
“Hey, look who it is!”
I turned toward the gravelly voice. Some hairy guy was grinning at me.
“Taekyung. You’re Jin Taekyung, right?”
“Uncle Kkeokjeong?”
This guy’s still alive?
His surname was Im. I’d forgotten his given name. I was pretty sure I’d heard it once, when he introduced himself seven years ago, but I couldn’t remember it.
He looked so much like a bandit that everyone called him Im Kkeokjeong.
“How’ve you been all this time?”
“Life as an F-rank Hunter is pretty much the same for all of us. How about you?”
“Don’t call me uncle.”
Im Kkeokjeong gave me an easy smile.
“Call me hyung. We’re not even that far apart in age.”
How many years apart were we again? I couldn’t quite remember.
“Hyung, how old are you?”
“Forty-five.”
What’s with that confidence?
But the social skills I’d honed over the years came through for me. I somehow managed to force a smile.
“You’re right. I’ll just call you hyung.”
“That’s it, little brother. Hahahaha!”
His hearty laughter rang through the hall. Nearly a hundred people looked over, then turned away.
I should’ve just pretended I didn’t hear him and kept walking.
Ours wasn’t exactly a deep connection. We’d seen each other almost every day for about half a year at the Ilsan office and worked together a few times. That was about it.
He’s a good guy, but...
Sometimes it was embarrassing to be around him.
Like now.
“The yulmu tea here is incredible. The chairs in the hall are nice and soft too.”
Im Kkeokjeong tossed back his yulmu tea in one gulp and leaned his chair as far back as it would go.
Judging by how comfortable he looked, this clearly wasn’t his first or second visit.
“You come here often?”
“Not every day. I drop by now and then. Once I got married and had kids, I started being more careful. Heh heh.”
Apparently, he’d started a family while we were out of touch. When I congratulated him, Im Kkeokjeong scratched his head.
“What’s so special about that?”
He was being modest, but a big deal was a big deal. He’d worked as a Hunter—an F-rank Hunter—for more than twenty years and still managed to build a family.
I wondered if the Im Kkeokjeong in front of me might be my future self.
Assuming I live to that age.
Being a Hunter wasn’t a career you could keep up for long. Plenty of people retired the moment they completed the ten years needed to qualify for a pension.
“Anyway, you’re starting to look the part. When I first met you, you were so nervous you could barely talk.”
“Of course. I’ve got seven years under my belt now.”
“So you’ve been bouncing around manpower offices ever since? Didn’t you sign a fairly decent contract with some small or midsize Guild? So, So... what was it called again?”
“Sopung Guild. They fired me the day before yesterday.”
Im Kkeokjeong forced a laugh.
“Hahaha! Good for you. The Guild’s name was lousy anyway. Sopung? What kind of name is that? It’s not like you’re going on a picnic to a Gate.”
“No, not that kind of sopung. It’s a place name. They’re near Bucheon Sopung Terminal, so they’re called Sopung Guild.”

The conversation that followed was surprisingly useful. Im Kkeokjeong was a regular at the manpower office, after all, and a veteran Hunter with good information and plenty of hard-earned tricks of the trade.
“The office takes a ten percent commission. That’s standard. But this branch has a pretty good batting average.”
Batting average was industry slang for your odds of getting hired. For someone whose immediate goal was a day’s pay, that was good news.
“Even for F-rank Hunters like us?”
“Huh? Yeah. That’s right.”
What’s with that awkward look?
Before I could ask anything else, a voice came through the speakers in the hall.
“E-rank Hunter Im Hyeokjun. Im Hyeokjun, please come to the lobby.”
Six thirty in the morning.
At last, the first batter was up. My turn would come only after all the E-rank Hunters had gone.
“E-ranks first, as expected... Hyung, where are you going?”
“I’ll go on ahead.”
Im Kkeokjeong—or rather, Im Hyeokjun—slung a large bag of armor and weapons over his shoulder and chuckled.
No wonder his expression looked off.
He must have worked himself to the bone while we were out of touch.
It was only a single step up, but advancing beyond F-rank despite an F-rank’s potential was no easy feat.
“See you around.”
“Yeah. See you.”
His departure from the hall opened the floodgates. The speakers began rattling off names one after another.
E-rank so-and-so, E-rank somebody else, E-rank...
Goddamn it, am I the only F-rank here?
Just as I was starting to get anxious—
“F-rank Hunter Jin Taekyung. Jin Taekyung, please come to the lobby.”
There it is!
“Mr. Jin Taekyung?”
A man in a white linen shirt was waiting in the lobby. Without so much as a greeting, he held out a contract, his expression flat.
“I’m from the Peace Guild. Read it and sign.”
This guy’s tone is seriously irritating.
I glared from the contract to the man’s face and back.
“The settlement split is eight to two.”
“After the raid, the proceeds will be distributed fairly according to contribution. We’ll take twenty percent of your share.”
“And the base pay?”
“Thirty.”
“Thir...ty?”
Did this guy lose half his tongue?
“Gate rank?”
“E-rank.”
“Rejected.”
“The combat positions are full. You’ll be a porter.”
The corner of my eye twitched.
What the hell did this guy just say?
“A por-ter?”
“Is there a problem?”
“Obviously.”
The man in the linen shirt glared down his nose at me.
“What is it?”
“I don’t have a pen.”
After a brief silence, I took the pen he handed me and scrawled my signature. The base pay was 300,000 won, and the settlement split was generous too.
I’d flinched when I heard it was an E-rank Gate, but I was only going as a porter, so it didn’t matter. I’d skin a few monsters, haul a pack around, then part ways with everyone in a good mood.
Peace Guild. I like the name already.
I’d been itching to sign so badly my fingers had almost cramped.
“All done.”
“So where are we going? Are we taking a van?”
“There’s one waiting outside.”
“Oh, that one? Looks nice. Bet the AC works great too.”
“Guess I was the last one. There are already a few people here... Huh? Kkeokjeong hyung!”
“Huh? Taekyung!”
Im Kkeokjeong was waiting to load his bags into the bus’s trunk. He grinned wide.
“You’re coming too. That’s great!”
“Looks like you and I really do have a connection, hyung.”
“Hahahaha!”
“Ahahaha!”
“...Let’s get going.”
Maybe it was the heat, but the man in the linen shirt suddenly looked years older.
The bus pulled out. From the passenger seat, the shirt guy said we’d arrive within twenty minutes, then closed his eyes.
Im Kkeokjeong introduced me to the others who’d been hired with us.
“All right, everyone, say hello. This is a younger friend of mine.”
Now that I looked, they all knew each other. I dipped my head.
“Hello. I’m Jin Taekyung.”
“Oh, nice to meet you.”
“Tall, handsome young fellow. Looks like he can fight.”
There were three new faces, all men in their late thirties or early forties. As the warm introductions continued, Im Kkeokjeong explained.
“These guys are all E-rank. I’ve known them for a long time. More than ten years now.”
“Yeah, about that long. Time sure flies.”
That meant every one of them had at least ten years of experience. I’d been around long enough that nobody would call me a rookie, but these guys were on another level.
A whole party of old-timers.
People like them pulled their weight wherever they went. In an emergency, they were far more dependable than some half-baked D-rank.
“So what rank are you, young man?”
Here it came. The rank check.
I answered carefully.
“F-rank.”
“Ah. That so? How long have you been at it?”
“Seven years.”
“Hmm. That so?”
The mood went lukewarm. If my first raid started like this, that would be a problem.
I ran my mouth before it could settle.
“I won’t be taking part in combat. I’m joining as a porter, so you don’t need to worry...”
The three men stared blankly at me.
“Why the long explanation? You think we’re going to eat you?”
“Drop it. If he’s been knocking around for seven years, he knows enough.”
“If Kkeokjeong hyung recommended him, that’s good enough. Team Leader Choi must’ve thought he was all right too, or he wouldn’t have agreed.”
Recommended? Team Leader Choi?
I didn’t know the exact details, but I could more or less piece together what had happened.
Im Kkeokjeong had recommended me to the man in the linen shirt—Team Leader Choi.
“W-what are you talking about?”
Im Kkeokjeong waved his hands, his face turning bright red.
The three men snickered.
“It’s written all over your face. How did this hyung ever manage to get married?”
“Good deeds are supposed to come to light. Why hide them?”
“Exactly. You think so too, don’t you?”
I nodded at once.
“Of course. Thank you for looking out for me.”
“Ahem. I just put in a word. Team Leader Choi made the decision.”
Well, then...

I’d thought of Im Kkeokjeong as one of the countless people I’d briefly crossed paths with and then moved on from. Meeting him again, I realized he was far more guileless and warmhearted than I’d expected.
So that’s why the terms were so generous.
Judging by the way they kept mentioning Team Leader Choi, I figured their friendship had played a part in my contract too.
“I’ll work hard.”
“I told you, Team Leader Choi made the decision!”
The man in question answered Im Kkeokjeong’s awkward excuse.
“Then let’s say I made the decision.”
The man in the linen shirt had opened his eyes at some point. No—Team Leader Choi. He addressed us.
“We’re here.”
I turned my head. A four-meter-high Gate loomed closer. At its center, a vortex of magical power churned, ready to suck us in.
An E-rank Gate.
My first raid since coming back.

sentences.text: The Hunter Manpower Office.
They called it an office, but it occupied an entire six-story building on prime real estate right by the station.
Hundreds of Hunters passed through its doors every day.
It’s been a while.
Even at dawn, the lobby was packed.
After waiting through the long line, I reached the counter.
The woman behind it asked in a businesslike tone,
“Is this your first time at the manpower office?”
“No.
I’m already registered.”
“Your name?”
“Jin Taekyung.”
Back when I was a rookie, I’d graduated from the Hunter Training Center with excellent scores.
But hardly anyone needed an F-rank Hunter like me, and the contracts a few small and midsize Guilds offered as if they were doing me a favor were highway robbery.
So I’d come here instead.
To a different branch, though.
“There’s a record at the Ilsan branch.
I’ve put you on the list, so please wait in the hall on the first floor.”
“Yes.”
This six-story building was a pyramid unto itself.
The first floor took E- and F-ranks.
You needed to be at least D-rank to set foot on the second.
Some people got angry and asked if that wasn’t blatant discrimination.
It was.
Not like this was the first or second time.
I’d lasted seven years in this business and seen every ugly side of it.
I’d long since passed the point where I could afford to be picky.
I had just started walking when—
“Hey, look who it is!”
I turned toward the gravelly voice.
Some hairy guy was grinning at me.
“Taekyung.
You’re Jin Taekyung, right?”
“Uncle Kkeokjeong?”
This guy’s still alive?
His surname was Im.
I’d forgotten his given name.
I was pretty sure I’d heard it once, when he introduced himself seven years ago, but I couldn’t remember it.
He looked so much like a bandit that everyone called him Im Kkeokjeong.
“How’ve you been all this time?”
“Life as an F-rank Hunter is pretty much the same for all of us.
How about you?”
“Don’t call me uncle.”
Im Kkeokjeong gave me an easy smile.
“Call me hyung.
We’re not even that far apart in age.”
How many years apart were we again?
I couldn’t quite remember.
“Hyung, how old are you?”
“Forty-five.”
What’s with that confidence?
But the social skills I’d honed over the years came through for me.
I somehow managed to force a smile.
“You’re right.
I’ll just call you hyung.”
“That’s it, little brother.
Hahahaha!”
His hearty laughter rang through the hall.
Nearly a hundred people looked over, then turned away.
I should’ve just pretended I didn’t hear him and kept walking.
Ours wasn’t exactly a deep connection.
We’d seen each other almost every day for about half a year at the Ilsan office and worked together a few times.
That was about it.
He’s a good guy, but...
Sometimes it was embarrassing to be around him.
Like now.
“The yulmu tea here is incredible.
The chairs in the hall are nice and soft too.”
Im Kkeokjeong tossed back his yulmu tea in one gulp and leaned his chair as far back as it would go.
Judging by how comfortable he looked, this clearly wasn’t his first or second visit.
“You come here often?”
“Not every day.
I drop by now and then.
Once I got married and had kids, I started being more careful.
Heh heh.”
Apparently, he’d started a family while we were out of touch.
When I congratulated him, Im Kkeokjeong scratched his head.
“What’s so special about that?”
He was being modest, but a big deal was a big deal.
He’d worked as a Hunter—an F-rank Hunter—for more than twenty years and still managed to build a family.
I wondered if the Im Kkeokjeong in front of me might be my future self.
Assuming I live to that age.
Being a Hunter wasn’t a career you could keep up for long.
Plenty of people retired the moment they completed the ten years needed to qualify for a pension.
“Anyway, you’re starting to look the part.
When I first met you, you were so nervous you could barely talk.”
“Of course.
I’ve got seven years under my belt now.”
“So you’ve been bouncing around manpower offices ever since?
Didn’t you sign a fairly decent contract with some small or midsize Guild?
So, So... what was it called again?”
“Sopung Guild.
They fired me the day before yesterday.”
Im Kkeokjeong forced a laugh.
“Hahaha!
Good for you.
The Guild’s name was lousy anyway.
Sopung?
What kind of name is that?
It’s not like you’re going on a picnic to a Gate.”
“No, not that kind of sopung.
It’s a place name.
They’re near Bucheon Sopung Terminal, so they’re called Sopung Guild.”
The conversation that followed was surprisingly useful.
Im Kkeokjeong was a regular at the manpower office, after all, and a veteran Hunter with good information and plenty of hard-earned tricks of the trade.
“The office takes a ten percent commission.
That’s standard.
But this branch has a pretty good batting average.”
Batting average was industry slang for your odds of getting hired.
For someone whose immediate goal was a day’s pay, that was good news.
“Even for F-rank Hunters like us?”
“Huh?
Yeah.
That’s right.”
What’s with that awkward look?
Before I could ask anything else, a voice came through the speakers in the hall.
“E-rank Hunter Im Hyeokjun.
Im Hyeokjun, please come to the lobby.”
Six thirty in the morning.
At last, the first batter was up.
My turn would come only after all the E-rank Hunters had gone.
“E-ranks first, as expected...
Hyung, where are you going?”
“I’ll go on ahead.”
Im Kkeokjeong—or rather, Im Hyeokjun—slung a large bag of armor and weapons over his shoulder and chuckled.
No wonder his expression looked off.
He must have worked himself to the bone while we were out of touch.
It was only a single step up, but advancing beyond F-rank despite an F-rank’s potential was no easy feat.
“See you around.”
“Yeah.
See you.”
His departure from the hall opened the floodgates.
The speakers began rattling off names one after another.
E-rank so-and-so, E-rank somebody else, E-rank...
Goddamn it, am I the only F-rank here?
Just as I was starting to get anxious—
“F-rank Hunter Jin Taekyung.
Jin Taekyung, please come to the lobby.”
There it is!
“Mr.
Jin Taekyung?”
A man in a white linen shirt was waiting in the lobby.
Without so much as a greeting, he held out a contract, his expression flat.
“I’m from the Peace Guild.
Read it and sign.”
This guy’s tone is seriously irritating.
I glared from the contract to the man’s face and back.
“The settlement split is eight to two.”
“After the raid, the proceeds will be distributed fairly according to contribution.
We’ll take twenty percent of your share.”
“And the base pay?”
“Thirty.”
“Thir...ty?”
Did this guy lose half his tongue?
“Gate rank?”
“E-rank.”
“Rejected.”
“The combat positions are full.
You’ll be a porter.”
The corner of my eye twitched.
What the hell did this guy just say?
“A por-ter?”
“Is there a problem?”
“Obviously.”
The man in the linen shirt glared down his nose at me.
“What is it?”
“I don’t have a pen.”
After a brief silence, I took the pen he handed me and scrawled my signature.
The base pay was 300,000 won, and the settlement split was generous too.
I’d flinched when I heard it was an E-rank Gate, but I was only going as a porter, so it didn’t matter.
I’d skin a few monsters, haul a pack around, then part ways with everyone in a good mood.
Peace Guild.
I like the name already.
I’d been itching to sign so badly my fingers had almost cramped.
“All done.”
“So where are we going?
Are we taking a van?”
“There’s one waiting outside.”
“Oh, that one?
Looks nice.
Bet the AC works great too.”
“Guess I was the last one.
There are already a few people here...
Huh?
Kkeokjeong hyung!”
“Huh?
Taekyung!”
Im Kkeokjeong was waiting to load his bags into the bus’s trunk.
He grinned wide.
“You’re coming too.
That’s great!”
“Looks like you and I really do have a connection, hyung.”
“Hahahaha!”
“Ahahaha!”
“...Let’s get going.”
Maybe it was the heat, but the man in the linen shirt suddenly looked years older.
The bus pulled out.
From the passenger seat, the shirt guy said we’d arrive within twenty minutes, then closed his eyes.
Im Kkeokjeong introduced me to the others who’d been hired with us.
“All right, everyone, say hello.
This is a younger friend of mine.”
Now that I looked, they all knew each other.
I dipped my head.
“Hello.
I’m Jin Taekyung.”
“Oh, nice to meet you.”
“Tall, handsome young fellow.
Looks like he can fight.”
There were three new faces, all men in their late thirties or early forties.
As the warm introductions continued, Im Kkeokjeong explained.
“These guys are all E-rank.
I’ve known them for a long time.
More than ten years now.”
“Yeah, about that long.
Time sure flies.”
That meant every one of them had at least ten years of experience.
I’d been around long enough that nobody would call me a rookie, but these guys were on another level.
A whole party of old-timers.
People like them pulled their weight wherever they went.
In an emergency, they were far more dependable than some half-baked D-rank.
“So what rank are you, young man?”
Here it came.
The rank check.
I answered carefully.
“F-rank.”
“Ah.
That so?
How long have you been at it?”
“Seven years.”
“Hmm.
That so?”
The mood went lukewarm.
If my first raid started like this, that would be a problem.
I ran my mouth before it could settle.
“I won’t be taking part in combat.
I’m joining as a porter, so you don’t need to worry...”
The three men stared blankly at me.
“Why the long explanation?
You think we’re going to eat you?”
“Drop it.
If he’s been knocking around for seven years, he knows enough.”

Recommended?
Team Leader Choi?
I didn’t know the exact details, but I could more or less piece together what had happened.

chapters.title: Chapter 42
paragraphs: A Gate.
The greatest mark left by the Great Cataclysm.

More than thirty years ago, Demon King Asmodeus had used Gates as invasion routes. They had long since become a means for Hunters to make a living and excavation sites for Magic Gems, a higher-dimensional energy resource.
“You’re with the Peace Guild, correct?”
A middle-aged man in work clothes approached us from the entrance.
He was a civil servant with the Gate Management Office, which stationed officials at every Gate.
“Yes.”
The official nodded at Team Leader Choi’s curt reply.
“You’re right on time. When will you be entering?”
“We’ll gear up and go straight in.”
“There’s a waiting room on the second floor. Come back down once you’re ready. Well, then.”
We followed Team Leader Choi inside. The two-story building housing the Management Office was as run-down as they came, and the waiting room wasn’t much better.
Holy shit. That smell.
The moment we opened the door, the stench of sweat hit me. Rusty cabinets and an overflowing trash can jumped out at me too.
“This place is awful. Don’t they ever air it out?”
“That’s Gate officials for you. There’s a reason everyone calls this a cushy posting.”
I left the grumbling behind and started changing into my raid gear. Leather armor and lightweight combat boots. Last, I drew a spear from its long case and gripped it.
It’s been a while.
The way it fit snugly in my hand felt both familiar and strange.
It was definitely different from the weapon I’d used for the past month... No. Never mind. I shouldn’t think about that anymore.
I have to forget all of it now.
I was tightening the perfectly fine laces on my combat boots for no reason when Im Kkeokjeong came over.
Clad in full-body armor and carrying an enormous tower shield, he looked every bit the main tank.
“All ready?”
“Yeah. Pretty much.”
Im Kkeokjeong looked me up and down, then clicked his tongue.
“Look at this guy. How old is that equipment, even?”
“Who knows? I bought it when I first started, so at least seven years?”
Back when I was a rookie, I’d taken the plunge and bought it from an underground shop in Dongdaemun. I still remembered the exact price.
1.98 million won.
I could barely sleep for days after buying it.
Hunters earned a lot, but they spent a lot too, and most of those expenses went toward equipment. It was all because of the unique nature of Gates.
Equipment that isn’t imbued with mana or magical power breaks down in no time.
So the most common method was to craft equipment from Magic Gems taken from Gate monsters.
The higher the Grade of the Magic Gem, the more the price shot through the roof.
“Seven years? Good grief. Saving money is all well and good, but you’ve got to spend it when it counts. You really want to pinch pennies when your life’s on the line?”
“Hmm. I had my reasons.”
Reasons I didn’t particularly want to discuss. Im Kkeokjeong spoke in a concerned voice.
“You’re in a noncombat position today, so you should be fine... but be careful.”
“I will.”
His words left me with a strange feeling. They reminded me of someone who, until recently, had constantly been telling me to be careful.
But the sentimentality didn’t last.
“Is everyone ready?”
Team Leader Choi appeared, and my jaw dropped.
No way.
“Is that a Red Drake leather set?”
“Hmm.”
Team Leader Choi’s face stiffened. I’d only ever seen gear like that in luxury catalogs, and the words had slipped out before I could stop them.
“Ah, sorry...”
“It’s nothing special. It was merely crafted using five types of magic and B-grade Magic Gems.”
“Not that I’m emphasizing the point, but its materials include five types of magic and B-grade Magic Gems.”
“Ah. Right.”
“Red Drake leather is popular for its distinctive sheen, but it only looks impressive. It isn’t particularly useful.”
Team Leader Choi moved, his face still stiff. A faint red glow flashed across him.
“But it is exceptionally beautiful.”
“Let’s head downstairs.”
Team Leader Choi left the waiting room first. Im Kkeokjeong sidled over to me.
“That guy loves it when someone recognizes his equipment.”
“I mean, I get that, but... what’s with him?”
“No idea. He’s an equipment nut. There’s even a rumor that he blew his entire fortune on that set and sleeps in it every night.”
So that bastard’s a nutjob too.
I sighed inwardly and prayed that today’s raid would end without incident.
“This isn’t the same number of people you registered.”
The civil servant looked uncomfortable. Fair enough. We were supposed to enter soon, and the party still wasn’t all there.
How much longer are we supposed to wait?
Only six people had gathered in front of the Gate. Excluding me, the porter, that left just five combatants.
Since this was an E-rank Gate, we needed at least five more Hunters of the same rank... but those Peace Guild bastards were nowhere in sight. No wonder the official was annoyed.
“You should’ve notified us in advance if you were adding personnel.”
Huh? What did he just say?
Adding personnel?
“I’m sorry.”
At Team Leader Choi’s curt apology, the official picked up his pen and drew several lines through the paperwork.
“It’s not a major problem since we can amend it... but please be more careful next time.”
“Yes.”
Not a major problem, my ass. There aren’t any people!
I poked Im Kkeokjeong in the ribs.
“Hyung. When are the others getting here?”
“What others?”
“The Peace Guild members.”
“Team Leader Choi’s right there.”
“What?”
“Oh, did I forget to tell you? The Peace Guild is new, so it doesn’t have many people. There are only three of us, including the Guild Master. Hahaha!”
...You’re laughing?
“Come on, hyung.”
“I know, punk. But you don’t need to worry.”
Im Kkeokjeong patted my shoulder and pointed at Team Leader Choi, who was signing the paperwork.
“That man’s a C-rank Hunter.”
“Oh. C-rank...”
I shut my mouth.

If Team Leader Choi was a C-rank Hunter, there was no problem. No, he was far better than ten E-rank Hunters. He was a mid-rank Hunter, in a completely different league from a low-rank Hunter like me.
I should’ve realized the moment I saw him wearing that luxury gear.
The man was walking around with a high-end apartment wrapped around his body. Most low-rank Hunters couldn’t afford armor like that even if they cleaned out their entire fortunes ten times over.
A faint halo seemed to shine around Team Leader Choi’s back.
“Please verify the signature.”
Even the way he handed the pen back to the official looked elegant.
Every little movement seemed to ooze wealth.
So this is the dignity of a C-rank Hunter.
That’s fucking cool.
I wanted to become sworn brothers with him. To pledge brotherhood beneath the Gate—a gay oath, no, a Gate oath.
“All right, then. Let’s go in... What is it?”
Team Leader Choi looked at me, startled.
“No. I just thought you looked cool.”
“Excuse me?”
“Your equipment. I said it looks cool.”
At that moment, the corner of Team Leader Choi’s mouth twitched.
“It’s nothing special. It was merely crafted using five types of magic and B-grade Magic Gems...”
A nutjob I wanted to befriend.
I stepped toward the Gate.
Whoosh—
A familiar sensation enveloped me. The cool, viscous energy unique to magical power.
Then the scenery changed.
“It’s a cave.”
Just as Team Leader Choi said, the raid site was a cave. The moisture-laden walls were damp, and a faint darkness shrouded our surroundings.
“Mr. Taekyung. Take out a flashlight.”
“Yes.”

I quickly set down my backpack. It was a porter’s bag Team Leader Choi had handed me just before we entered the Gate. It looked ordinary on the outside, but it was an expensive item enchanted with both space expansion and weight-reduction magic.
“Here’s the flashlight.”
I handed it over as requested, though in my experience, flashlights weren’t the best option. They were convenient, but if the light suddenly went out, your eyes wouldn’t be adjusted to the darkness.
It was much better to wait a little and let your eyes get used to the darkness...
Click.
“Let there be light. Light.”
Whoosh. A ball of light the size of a soccer ball shot from the flashlight and plastered itself against the cave ceiling.
“...Magic?”

“It has a built-in spell that activates as soon as the incantation is spoken. It lasts quite a while, so it should be good for another three or four hours. It’s a limited-edition item I purchased from Company M...”
Im Kkeokjeong summed it up.
“It’s crazy expensive.”
Was it my imagination, or had Team Leader Choi’s face darkened slightly? Maybe it was just the shadows.
Either way, the raid had become much easier thanks to him.
Money really is the best.
Capital ruled the world, and Gates were no exception. People with money fought in comfort using enchanted equipment. People without it carried torches.
“Take your positions.”

At Team Leader Choi’s command, everyone moved at once. Im Kkeokjeong and another E-rank Hunter took the lead as tanks, with Team Leader Choi behind them. I, the porter, and the two ranged dealers stood at the very back.
“Move.”
We began advancing slowly.
The bright magical light illuminated the path ahead.
I want one.
“Kiiiieet!”
The creatures crouching in the darkness emerged with shrill cries. Green skin, squat bodies, and grotesque limbs.
They were Hobgoblins, an evolved form of ordinary goblin.
About thirty of them.
With only five combatants, this would be a difficult fight.
But having a C-rank Hunter changes everything.
On top of that, the other four were veteran E-rank Hunters with at least ten-odd years of experience each.
I hung well back and watched the battle.
“Ranged!”
Arrows flew the instant Team Leader Choi gave the order.
One shot, one kill.
The arrows buried themselves in vital points, dropping the unshielded Hobgoblins one after another.
“Kiit!”
“Oh, look. Shield-bearers. What do we do?”
“Hold.”
Team Leader Choi issued his next command.
“Tanks, advance.”
The tanks moved forward in thick full-body armor, tower shields raised. Im Kkeokjeong and the other man were both hulking giants over 190 centimeters tall. The sight of them alone was intimidating.
“Kiiiieet!”
But monsters were monsters for a reason. Trusting in their numbers, the Hobgoblins charged like a swarm of bees.
But—
“Well, look at you.”
Bam!
The big, beautiful tower shields sent them flying back as bloody pulp. Seizing the momentum, Im Kkeokjeong swung his mace like a flyswatter, shattering limbs and crushing skulls with every blow.
“You punk! You punk!”
...What was this, whack-a-mole?
Veterans, all right.
All four of them stayed within their roles without overextending themselves, steadily whittling down the enemy numbers.
Knowing when to fall back and when to push in was combat intelligence born of plenty of experience.
“Everyone, hold your positions.”
And then one man.
The man who had been directing the flow of battle until now moved.
“I’ll take care of the rest.”
A red streak flashed across his armor as he plunged into the twenty remaining Hobgoblins.
Slash—
A head soared into the air along a clean arc. It happened so quickly that the monsters couldn’t even react.
“Kiiie?”
Slash. Slash. Slash.
The blade never stopped. Merciless and efficient, it pierced and severed one vital point after another.
This was no longer a battle.
It was a massacre—one man slaughtering more than twenty monsters.
So this is a C-rank Hunter.
His speed. His strength.
I could see it all. And I could feel it.
He really is strong.
As a mere F-rank, I couldn’t even dream of matching him. He was a mid-rank Hunter, three full ranks above me. A broad river and a towering wall that effort alone could never overcome.
Yet at the same time, a question arose.
What if this were Murim?
Team Leader Choi was unquestionably strong. He had the abilities befitting a C-rank Hunter and plenty of experience.
But if this were Murim... if he were a martial artist...
I’d be stronger.
His movements were fast and powerful, but that was all. He hadn’t learned martial arts, nor did he use his mana efficiently.
At best, he was First Rate. In Murim, that was exactly where he would stand.
But this is reality.
I bit my lip without realizing it.
A mid-rank Hunter and a bottom-rank Hunter.
While the mid-rank Hunter wore expensive equipment and slaughtered monsters, the lowest-rank Hunter could only stare blankly.
As a porter.
“Kiiieet...”
The last Hobgoblin fell. Team Leader Choi pulled his sword from its chest, and our eyes met.
“Mr. Taekyung. Please handle the byproducts.”
“Mr. Taekyung?”
I wanted to tell him that I was stronger than him.
But in the end, I couldn’t. Because this was my reality.
“...Thank you for your hard work.”
I used to be stronger than you.
